reason: The sources provide over 15 corroborating claims from multiple sites covering Barnard's Star's record speed, history, and planet-hunting saga.
story: In 1916, astronomer E. E. Barnard tracked a faint red dwarf in the constellation Ophiuchus and discovered something extraordinary: it was streaking across our night sky faster than any other known star. Located just six light-years away, Barnard's Star is our Sun's closest neighbor after the Alpha Centauri system. Yet despite its proximity, it is far too dim to see without a telescope. What makes it legendary is its blisteringly fast apparent motion, covering the width of the full Moon every 180 years as it races toward us at 110 kilometers per second. For over half a century, the star haunted astronomers with ghost planets—first in the 1960s with Peter van de Kamp's flawed wobble claims, and again in 2018 when a heralded super-Earth turned out to be mere stellar activity. Only in 2024 and 2025 did astronomers finally confirm genuine worlds: a system of tiny sub-Earth planets.
angle: Barnard's Star moves across our night sky faster than any other star in the universe, crossing the width of the full Moon in just 180 years.

claims.claim: Barnard's Star is named after American astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard.
In 1916, E. E. Barnard measured the star's rapid motion across the sky.
Barnard's Star has the fastest proper motion across the night sky of any star known.
Barnard's Star travels an apparent angular distance equivalent to the Moon's diameter roughly every 180 years.
The star is located in the constellation Ophiuchus.
Barnard's Star is classified as a red dwarf star.
The star is located roughly six light-years away from Earth.
Barnard's Star is the closest star system to the Sun after the Alpha Centauri system.
Barnard's Star has an apparent visual magnitude of around 9.5 and cannot be seen with the unaided eye.
The star's total space velocity relative to the Sun is approximately 143 km/s (around 500,000 km/h).
Barnard's Star is blueshifted and moving toward the Sun with a radial velocity of roughly 110 km/s.
In the 1960s, astronomer Peter van de Kamp claimed astrometric wobbles proved giant planets were orbiting Barnard's Star.
Peter van de Kamp's planetary claims were debunked in the 1970s as telescope artifacts and errors.
In November 2018, astronomers announced the detection of a candidate super-Earth orbiting Barnard's Star every 233 days with a minimum mass of 3.2 Earth masses.
The 2018 super-Earth candidate was later refuted after its signal was found to stem from the star's own activity.
Real exoplanets orbiting Barnard's Star were confirmed in 2024 and 2025 using radial velocity measurements.

disputed: Closest approach timing: S1 states Barnard's Star will reach its closest approach of 3.75 light-years around 11,800 CE, whereas S5 reports a closest approach of 3.9 light-years in just under 10,000 years. The script should mention 'in roughly 10,000 to 12,000 years' rather than asserting a single figure.

Refuted super-Earth estimated temperature: S2 estimates the 2018 candidate planet at -170 °C, while S4 and S7 state -150 °C. Because the planet was disproven, this detail should be avoided or described as a disputed estimate of the phantom world.
